blocks.text:
WhatsApp is built around a private conversation between two people, or a small group. Slack is built around something structurally different: a persistent, searchable team workspace organized into channels, where messages are not fleeting but form a durable record the whole team can search through months later. A message posted to a busy channel needs to reach everyone currently online instantly, while someone who logs in the next morning needs to catch up cleanly from wherever they left off, and anyone at all needs to be able to search across the entire history of every channel they belong to for a phrase they vaguely remember from three weeks ago.

We are going to design the core of a team messaging platform: workspaces containing channels, real-time message delivery to every connected device, a lightweight way to track what a user has and has not read, threaded replies, and full-text search across message history.

blocks.text: Suppose a workspace platform has 5 million daily active users across all workspaces, each posting a modest average of 20 messages a day and reading roughly 10 times that many. That is 5,000,000 times 20, or 100 million messages posted per day, averaging 100,000,000 divided by 86,400, about 1,150 writes per second. Reads, at roughly 10 times that, land around 11,500 reads per second on average, spiking well higher during business hours across time zones.

blocks.title: Why a single read cursor instead of per-message read receipts
blocks.text: WhatsApp needs per-message delivery and read receipts because a 1:1 or small group conversation is short enough that tracking every message's state individually is cheap and the sender genuinely wants to know "did they see THIS message." A busy Slack channel can have thousands of messages a day across thousands of members; tracking a read receipt per message per member would be an enormous amount of bookkeeping for a signal nobody actually needs at that granularity. A single last-read watermark per user per channel answers "how many unread messages do I have" just as well, at a small fraction of the storage and write cost.

A worked example diagram: Alice posts a message in a shared channel, and Bob, connected on both desktop and mobile, receives it instantly on both devices

blocks.text: Alice posts an update in the team's shared channel. The message service persists it and publishes it to the channel's pub-sub topic. Bob, who happens to have both his laptop and his phone connected at that moment, receives the message on both devices within a fraction of a second, since the pub-sub router fans out to every one of his active sessions, not just one. When Bob reads the message on his phone, his read cursor for that channel advances; the next time he glances at his laptop, its unread count for that channel has already caught up too, since the cursor lives server-side and is shared across every device he is connected from, not tracked independently per device.

blocks.text: The offline case matters just as much: if Bob had been fully disconnected when Alice posted, he simply fetches everything since his last cursor position the next time he opens the app, in the exact same order the messages were actually posted.

blocks.text: The most recent messages in an actively-viewed channel are cached, since a freshly opened channel almost always wants to show the latest handful of messages immediately. Read cursors, being tiny and frequently read, are also cached aggressively, since a per-device unread-count check happens far more often than a cursor actually advances.

blocks.text: Message delivery and search both lean toward availability with a small, bounded amount of eventual consistency. The one place needing real care is the read cursor: two devices racing to advance it should never leave a stale, backward-moving cursor in place, so cursor updates need a simple last-writer-wins-by-timestamp rule at minimum, ensuring the cursor only ever moves forward.

blocks.text: If a gateway instance fails, every connection it was holding drops and reconnects to another instance, catching up via the same read-cursor-based sync mechanism used for any offline period, so a gateway failure looks identical to a brief network blip from the client's perspective.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing the deliberate choice of server-side readable, encrypted at rest and in transit messages rather than end to end encryption, since search, compliance, and admin visibility are core requirements for a workplace tool

blocks.text: This is the most important security-adjacent design decision in the whole system, and it is worth stating plainly: messages here are not end-to-end encrypted. They are encrypted in transit and at rest, and access is protected by standard authentication and per-workspace authorization, but the server itself can read message content, because full-text search, legal compliance retention, and administrator visibility are genuine, load-bearing product requirements for a workplace communication tool, not afterthoughts. This is a direct, deliberate inversion of WhatsApp's end-to-end encrypted design, driven entirely by a different product context.

blocks.text: The single-watermark read cursor model (section 11) trades away per-message read visibility (you cannot know exactly which teammates have seen a specific message) for a dramatically simpler and cheaper unread-tracking system, the right trade for a busy team channel where that fine-grained signal is rarely needed. The choice not to end-to-end encrypt (section 21) trades away the strongest possible privacy guarantee for search, compliance, and administrative capabilities that are genuine requirements in a workplace context, an explicit product trade rather than an oversight.

items: A user connected on three devices simultaneously advances their read cursor from two of them at nearly the same moment, requiring the cursor update to be resolved so it only ever moves forward, never backward.
A message is posted to a channel with zero currently connected members, which should still persist and index normally, just with no real-time fan out to anyone.
A threaded reply is posted to a message that itself has since been deleted, requiring a defined behavior rather than an undefined error.
Search indexing falls behind during a sudden burst of messages, meaning a very recently posted message is briefly not yet searchable, which is an accepted, bounded staleness rather than a bug.
